title: Gaslighting in Relationships: Signs, Phrases, What to Do — cv.cm
description: What is gaslighting in a relationship? Common gaslighting phrases, how it differs from a normal disagreement, how to trust your memory, and where to get help.
h1: What is gaslighting in a relationship?
answer: Gaslighting is a form of emotional abuse where someone repeatedly makes you doubt your memory, perception or feelings so that you rely on their version of reality. It sounds like "That never happened" or "You're too sensitive". One disagreement about the past is not gaslighting. A pattern that leaves you confused, apologizing and unable to trust yourself is.

body: Gaslighting is not just lying. It is a repeated effort to make you doubt your own mind. Over time you may stop trusting what you saw, heard or felt, and start checking with the other person what is "real". That gives them power over you, and it can make leaving harder, because you no longer trust your own judgement.
The National Domestic Violence Hotline in the US groups common gaslighting tactics like this:

ul: Withholding: refusing to listen or pretending not to understand.
Countering: questioning your memory of events, even when you remember clearly.
Blocking or diverting: changing the subject or questioning your thinking instead of the issue.
Trivializing: treating your feelings as unimportant or as an overreaction.
Forgetting or denial: claiming not to remember, or denying promises and events.

body: Sociologist Paige Sweet has argued that gaslighting works best where there is already unequal power, for example around gender or money, because the person can use stereotypes such as "too emotional" or "irrational". It can happen to anyone, in any kind of couple, including same-sex relationships.

The word comes from the 1938 British stage play Gas Light by Patrick Hamilton, later made into films, the best known in 1944. In the story, a husband secretly dims the gas lamps in the house, and when his wife notices, he insists the light has not changed. He does this and other things to make her believe she is losing her mind.
The story fits because gaslighting is usually small and repeated, not one big lie. Each moment can seem minor. Together, they change how you see yourself.

sections.h: Common gaslighting phrases and what they do
body: Any of these can be said once in a normal argument. They become gaslighting when they are used often to dismiss your experience.

head: Phrase
What it does

rows: "That never happened."

"I remember it differently. I know what I saw."
"You're too sensitive."
Turns the problem into your feelings
"My feelings are real. I'm asking you to listen."
"You're imagining things."
Questions your perception
"I'm not imagining it. I'd like to talk about it."
"You're crazy." / "It's all in your head."
Attacks your sanity and credibility
"Please don't call me that. Let's talk about what happened."
"I was only joking."
Makes hurtful words seem harmless
"It didn't feel like a joke to me."
"Everyone agrees with me."
Isolates you and claims support
"I'd rather we talk about us."
"You always twist things."
Makes you doubt how you explain things
"I'm describing how it felt for me."
"If you loved me, you wouldn't bring this up."
Turns raising a concern into disloyalty
"I'm bringing it up because I care about us."

body.note: You do not need to win the argument about the past. A calm reply that holds your ground is enough. Then you can end the conversation.

sections.h: Gaslighting vs a normal disagreement about memory
body: Memory is imperfect. Couples often remember the same evening differently, and that is not abuse. These differences help you tell them apart.

sections.h: How to trust your own memory again
body: Gaslighting works by making you rely on the other person's version. These steps give you back your own.

ol: Keep a private record. Write the date, what happened and what was said, soon after it happens. Keep it somewhere the other person cannot read, such as a notes app with a lock, an email to yourself, or with a trusted friend.
Save important messages or screenshots if it is safe to do so.
Reality-check with people you trust. Describe events plainly to a friend, a family member or a counsellor and ask, "Does this sound okay to you?"
Notice your body. Constant confusion, anxiety, or feeling you must check everything are signs worth taking seriously.
Reduce arguments about "what really happened". You can say, "We remember it differently," and stop there.
Spend time with people and activities where you feel like yourself.

body: A record is for you, to steady your own view. It is not to win arguments or to show the other person, which can make things more dangerous if they react with anger.

sections.h: What to say in the moment
body: Short, calm sentences work better than long explanations. Some options:

ul: "I know what I experienced. I'm not going to argue about whether it happened."
"I hear that you see it differently. My feelings about it are still real."
"I'm not willing to continue this conversation if I'm being called crazy."
"I'm going to take a break and come back to this later."

body: If the person is willing to change, they will listen, admit mistakes at least sometimes, and the pattern will improve with time, often with help from a counsellor. If every attempt to talk turns into a debate about your sanity, that is information too.

sections.h: When to leave, and getting help
body: Gaslighting is emotional abuse. It often comes with other controlling behavior, such as checking your phone, cutting you off from friends, controlling money, or anger that frightens you. It is not your fault, and being gaslit does not mean you are weak or foolish. It is designed to be hard to see from the inside.

Consider getting support to leave, or leaving, if the pattern continues after you have named it, if you feel afraid, or if you notice you are losing touch with friends and with yourself. Couples counselling is often not recommended when one partner is abusive; individual support from a domestic-abuse service is usually safer.

body.note: If you are in danger now, contact your local emergency number. In the US, thehotline.org and loveisrespect.org offer free, confidential support by phone, text or chat; elsewhere, contact a domestic-violence helpline or a local service where you live. If you have thoughts of harming yourself, contact a crisis line or emergency services.

faq.q: Can someone gaslight without knowing it?
faq.a: Some people deny things out of defensiveness or shame, without a plan to control. The effect on you can still be harmful. The difference often shows when you name it: someone who did not intend harm can listen and change.

faq.q: Am I being gaslit or am I wrong?
faq.a: Everyone is wrong sometimes. If you can usually discuss mistakes on both sides and feel heard, it is probably normal disagreement. If you are almost always the one who is wrong and you feel more confused over time, take it seriously and talk to someone you trust.

faq.q: What are the long-term effects of gaslighting?
faq.a: People often describe anxiety, self-doubt, difficulty making decisions and feeling isolated. These usually improve with distance, support and time. A counsellor can help you rebuild trust in your own judgement.
Yes. Denying what was said, deleting messages, or insisting you misread a clear message can all be gaslighting. Saved messages can help you check your memory privately.

You can calmly name what you notice, but you do not have to prove anything. If the person has been frightening or violent, think about safety first and talk to a support service before any confrontation.
